title: Čech cohomology, Stokes' theorem and the de Rham theorem
summary: Refinement of covers and Čech cohomology; fine sheaves and the acyclicity of the sheaf of p-forms (§27, Definition 27.2); the Poincaré lemma implies that Čech and de Rham cohomology agree (§28); orientation, integration and Stokes' theorem from Hitchin §7; Smale's immersion theorem (lecture 35) as further reading.

objectives.description: Define the Čech differential and refinement maps, compute a cover cohomology, and prove acyclicity for the sheaf of smooth forms using a partition of unity.
Prove the Čech–de Rham comparison on good covers through the two exact directions of the double complex, stating the good-cover input.
Apply orientation and Stokes with the induced boundary signs, and synthesize the comparison on the sphere using a concrete good cover and a nonexact area form.

preparation.description: Read lecture 33: §26.1 refinement and §27 the acyclicity of the sheaf of p-forms, Definition 27.2 (fine sheaf).
Read lecture 34: §28 the Poincaré lemma implies the equality of Čech and de Rham cohomology.
Read Hitchin §7.1 (orientation) and §7.2 (Stokes' theorem), which the synthesis project uses to illustrate the theorem on a surface.

commonMisconceptions.claim: One constant per intersection always defines the Čech complex.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The coefficient sheaf consists of locally constant functions, so disconnected intersections need a constant on each component.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Acyclicity of smooth forms means all global closed forms are exact.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It is acyclicity in the Čech direction for the sheaf of forms. Global de Rham cohomology concerns the different differential d and can be nonzero.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The de Rham theorem recovers integral cohomology including torsion.
commonMisconceptions.correction: This comparison uses real coefficients. Integer torsion is not visible to differential forms with real coefficients.
